newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-Air France, Continental mull alliance - paper.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Air France, Continental mull alliance - paper.

text.p: French state-owned airline Air France and Continental Airlines are in the advanced stages of discussions on signing an alliance deal, the financial newspaper Les Echos said on Monday.
It quoted Continental chairman Gordon Bethune as telling U.S. specialised publication Aviation Daily that the talks were in their final stages but that no deal had been signed yet.
An Air France spokeswoman declined comment on the talks: "No comment," she said. "We are not announcing anything at all."
The paper said industry sources indicated that the French airline was talking to more than one airline about alliances, trying to find a good geographical spread to counter other airline alliances.
Les Echos said Air France talked to both Continental and USAir in the past few months.
Air France and Continental signed a commercial accord back in 1993 but it has never been implemented because of changes in top management at both companies.
Continental, among the U.S. majors, does not have a European partner.
Air France has previously said it was talking to Continental, as well as American Airlines of AMR Corp, United Airlines of UAL Corp, Delta Airlines Inc and USAir Group.
American has agreed a controversial alliance with British Airways Plc but regulatory approval has been held up by a row between the British and U.S. governments over an "open skies" agreement.

The planned BA-American alliance has been attacked by rivals as anti-competitive. Last month, Air France chairman Christian Blanc met U.S. Transportation Secretary Federico Pena to update him on the French company's negotiations on a U.S. partner.

The paper said the U.S. authorities were squaring up for another struggle with France over a bilateral "open skies" pact to allow greater market access, were preparing to refuse to authorise Air France's winter timetable and would also use any alliance deal as a lever to push the French to further open up the domestic market.

Washington and Paris clashed earlier this year when the United States wanted to open bilateral talks on market access and held up U.S. approval of Air France's summer schedule until the French agreed to start negotiations.
